title: Firm Foundations
subtitle: Two builders, one storm, and the part nobody can see.
objectives: Retell the parable of the wise and foolish builders
Explain what the rock and the sand stand for
Explain why both houses face the same storm
Explain the difference between hearing and doing
Identify one foundation habit to build this week

cards.title: Two builders who did almost everything the same
cards.text: Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with a short story about construction. Matthew 7, verses 24 to 27.

cards.title: What actually happens in it
cards.text: Two men build houses. The story spends no time on the houses at all, which is the first clue.
points: **One builds on rock.** One builds on sand.
**Rain, floods and wind** hit both houses.
**One stands. One falls**, and falls hard.
**The only difference mentioned** is the foundation.

cards.title: Same houses, same storm
cards.text: Tap through the three stages. The difference is invisible until the last one.

question.text: In the parable, what is the only stated difference between the two houses?
options: How long they took to build
question.explain: The foundation. The story never describes the houses themselves, and that is deliberate.

cards.title: Hearing is not the same as doing
cards.text: Jesus says the wise builder is the one who hears his words *and puts them into practice*. Both builders heard.
points: **Both men had the same information.**
**One acted on it. One did not.**
**James 1:22** says the same thing plainly.
**Knowing something** is not yet a foundation.

cards.title: This one is literally true in engineering
cards.text: Sand shifts under load and water. Rock does not. Every building code in the world starts with the ground.
points: **Foundations are the part nobody photographs.**
**They are also what everything else rests on.**
**A crack at the bottom** shows up at the top.
**The parable is not stretching anything.**

question.text: In the parable, only one of the two houses is hit by the storm.
question.explain: False. The rain, floods and wind come to both. The story is not about avoiding storms.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: The story is clear. Part 2 is what a foundation looks like in an actual week. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Nobody builds a foundation in one afternoon
cards.text: It is poured slowly, before anything visible exists, and while it is happening it looks like nothing is happening.

cards.title: Foundations are boring on purpose
cards.text: Anything that holds weight later is built early, repeatedly, and without an audience.
points: **Small and repeated** beats large and occasional.
**Nobody sees it** while it is being done.
**You find out whether it worked** under load.
**By then it is too late to start.**

cards.title: Your bones are doing this literally
cards.text: Bone density is built through your teens and locks in around your twenties. Nothing about it is visible while it happens.
points: **Built early, used for sixty years.**
**You cannot see it working.**
**The window does close.**
**Same shape as the parable**, in a body.

question.text: What does the wise builder do that the foolish one does not?
options: He puts what he heard into practice
He builds somewhere the storm cannot reach
question.explain: Both heard the same words. Only one acted on them, and that is the whole difference.

cards.title: Why he told it as a story at all
cards.text: He could have said "do what I said". Instead he built a picture you cannot argue with and will not forget.
points: **A rule gets debated.** A picture gets remembered.
**You can see both houses** without being told which is which.
**That is what a parable is for.**
**Worth knowing** when you write your own.

cards.title: One foundation, chosen on purpose
cards.text: The point of the parable is action, so the lesson ends with one. Pick something small enough to actually repeat.
points: **One habit, done daily**, beats five done once.
**Small enough that a bad day** does not break it.
**Write it down** where you will see it.
**Check it on Sunday.** Not before.

terms.def: A short story that teaches one point through a picture rather than a rule.
What everything else rests on. Built first, seen last.
In the parable, hearing Jesus' words and putting them into practice.
Hearing the same words and not acting on them.
The passage this parable comes from, at the end of the Sermon on the Mount.
Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. The same idea, stated plainly.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Two builders. One storm. One difference.**
**Both of them heard.** Only one acted.
**The storm comes either way.**
**Foundations are built before you need them.**

quiz.text: Where in the Bible is the parable of the two builders found?
quiz.explain: Matthew 7, at the very end of the Sermon on the Mount. Luke 6 tells it too.
quiz.objective: Retell the parable of the wise and foolish builders

quiz.text: What does the rock stand for in the parable?
options: Hearing Jesus' words and putting them into practice
Being wealthy enough to build well
quiz.explain: Hearing and doing. The foolish builder heard exactly the same words.
quiz.objective: Explain what the rock and the sand stand for

quiz.text: What does the sand stand for?
options: Hearing the words and not acting on them
quiz.explain: Both builders heard. The difference is only what they did afterwards.
quiz.objective: Explain what the rock and the sand stand for

quiz.text: In the parable, both houses face the same storm.
quiz.explain: True. Rain, floods and wind come to both. The story is not a promise of no storms.
quiz.objective: Explain why both houses face the same storm

quiz.text: Why does the story spend no time describing the houses?
options: Because the foundation is the only thing that matters to the point
Because Jesus was in a hurry
Because houses were all the same then
quiz.explain: Everything visible is left out. That is how the parable points at what is underneath.
quiz.objective: Retell the parable of the wise and foolish builders

quiz.text: Which verse states the hearing-and-doing idea plainly?
quiz.explain: James 1:22 — be doers of the word, and not hearers only.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between hearing and doing

quiz.text: Knowing what is right is the same as having a firm foundation.
quiz.explain: False. Both builders knew. The parable is about the gap between knowing and doing.
quiz.objective: Explain the difference between hearing and doing

quiz.text: Why are foundations described as invisible until they matter?
options: They are built underground, before anything visible exists
They are painted the same colour as the ground
They are added at the end of building
They are only in old buildings
quiz.explain: Poured first, covered up, and tested only under load. By then it is too late to start.
quiz.objective: Identify one foundation habit to build this week

quiz.text: What kind of habit makes the best foundation?
options: Small enough to repeat even on a bad day
Large enough to see progress immediately
One that only takes a single afternoon
quiz.explain: Small and repeated beats large and occasional. A bad day should not be able to break it.
quiz.objective: Identify one foundation habit to build this week

options: A short story that teaches one point through a picture
quiz.explain: A picture rather than a rule. A rule gets debated, a picture gets remembered.
quiz.objective: Retell the parable of the wise and foolish builders

items: One builds on rock, one on sand
One house stands and one falls
quiz.explain: Build, choose, storm, result. The choice is made long before the storm arrives.
quiz.objective: Retell the parable of the wise and foolish builders

quiz.text: The parable promises that a wise builder will not face storms.
quiz.explain: False. Both houses face the same weather. What differs is what happens next.
quiz.objective: Explain why both houses face the same storm

teacher.summary: Week 1 Devotion covers the parable of the wise and foolish builders, matching the Term 1 theme. The lesson is built around the two details students usually miss: both builders heard the same words, and both houses face the same storm. Without those, the parable gets read as a promise of protection rather than as a claim about the gap between hearing and doing. The rockOrSand figure shows both houses under one storm for exactly that reason. The engineering is not a stretch here — sand really does shift under load and water — so the car lens is used to make the parable concrete rather than to decorate it. The lesson ends on an action, because the parable does.
discussion: Ask him what the story would mean if only one house had been hit by the storm. It is the fastest way to the actual point.
Ask why Jesus told it as a story rather than as an instruction. A rule gets argued with; a picture does not.
Ask what a foundation habit would look like in his own week. Small enough to survive a bad day is the test.
Ask what other foundations he can think of that are invisible until they are tested.
teacher.extension: Have him choose one small daily habit, write it somewhere visible, and check it at the end of the week. The point of the parable is action, so the follow-through is the assignment rather than the reflection.
misconceptions: 'The wise builder avoided the storm.' Both houses face the same rain, floods and wind. That is stated in the passage.
'The foolish builder had never heard the words.' He heard exactly the same words. He did not act on them.
'A parable is a true story about real people.' It is a short story told to make one point through a picture.
'A foundation is something you can put in later.' It is built first and tested last, which is the whole warning.
